# Get the data

Our very first hands-on step: **get the dataset onto your machine and take a look
at it.** Everything you plot today comes from this data, so let's start here.

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> Pick a setup on the Welcome page first
  (cloud, your own computer, or with an AI assistant). Then come back here.
</div>

## The dataset {-}

We'll use a **real proteomics dataset** — peptide-level measurements from the
public study [PXD040621](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD040621).
It's a normal messy-ish table of real measurements, which is exactly what makes
it good practice.

## Download it {-}

There are two ways to get the data — use whichever matches your setup.

**A. You cloned the repo or you're in Codespaces**

Good news: the data is already there, in the `data-01/` folder. You can skip
straight to **Load it** below.

**B. You want to download it fresh**

Run this in R to create a `data-01/` folder and download the file into it:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Create a folder for the data (if it doesn't exist yet)
dir.create("data-01", showWarnings = FALSE)

# Download the dataset into data-01/
url <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/biosustain/dsp_workshop_datavizR/main/data-01/PXD040621_peptides.csv"
download.file(url, destfile = "data-01/PXD040621_peptides.csv", mode = "wb")
```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> <code>download.file()</code> saves the file to
  disk once. After that you just <em>read</em> it in R — you don't download it
  again.
</div>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"What does `mode = "wb"` do in `download.file()` in R, and
> when do I need it?"*

## Load it {-}

Now read the file into R as a data frame. We use `read_csv()` from the `readr`
package (part of the `tidyverse`).

```{r, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
data <- read_csv("../data-01/PXD040621_peptides.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(readr)
data <- read_csv("data-01/PXD040621_peptides.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

## First look {-}

Before plotting anything, always get a feel for your data. Try each of these:

```{r}
# How big is it? (rows, columns)
dim(data)
```

```{r}
# The first few rows
head(data)
```

```{r}
# A compact summary of every column: name, type, first values
dplyr::glimpse(data)
```

```{r}
# The column names on their own
names(data)
```

<div class="remember">
  <strong>📌 Remember:</strong> <code>glimpse()</code> is the fastest way to see
  <em>what columns you have and what type they are</em> — which is exactly what
  you need to know before choosing a plot.
</div>

> 🤖 **Ask your AI:** *"Here are my column names: `<paste output of names(data)>`.
> Which columns would make a good first scatter plot, and why?"*

**You're ready.** You now have the data loaded as `data`. In the next chapter we
start turning it into plots.
